summary: Ars Technica reports on a Harvard study (Fiona Chen and James Stratton) using Jellyfish engineering analytics from over 700 firms through March 2026. AI coding agents raised lines of code, commits and pull requests, but issue and epic resolution did not change significantly. Human code review is the bottleneck. The excerpt ends partway through the article.
speakers_or_authors: Ars Technica AI staff writer (byline not shown); study by Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton
relevance_reason: It is about AI coding agents and workplace output, with real measured evidence. But coding agents are not the computer-use, personal-context or voice interfaces the brief targets, and coding-model topics are largely excluded. At most it offers a useful analogy about agent output being limited by human review.

claims.claim: Study of hundreds of firms finds human code review is a bottleneck, with little evidence that AI tools raise software output or cut employment.
claims.quote: little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment

claims.claim: Adopting AI coding agents raised lines of code by 30%, commits by 20% and pull requests by 23% on average.
claims.quote: The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated

claims.claim: Resolution rates for Jira issues and epics showed no statistically significant change after AI tools were introduced.
claims.quote: the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way

claims.claim: Code review grew longer, with more revisions and more reviewer comments on pull requests.
claims.quote: the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.

commercial_interest: None evident. The data come from Jellyfish, an engineering analytics vendor, but the analysis was by independent Harvard researchers.
older_event: No. The study is recent (data through March 2026) and the article is dated October 2026.
